strengths: Addresses a clear and relevant gap: interpretability of visual prompt tuning, which prior interpretable part-prototype methods (ProtoPNet, TesNet, ProtoPool, etc.) do not cover. The claim of being the 'first framework' for interpretable visual prompt tuning appears well-supported by the related work.

The proposed method is technically coherent: concept prototypes grounded to image regions via Concept Region Discovery, feature aggregation into prompts (IFA), and a fine-to-coarse hierarchical prototype structure with a consistency loss are all described with sufficient detail to understand the mechanism.

Evaluation is reasonably comprehensive: five backbone variants (DeiT and DinoV2 at multiple scales), quantitative interpretability metrics (consistency and stability scores from Huang et al.) using CUB keypoint annotations unavailable at training time, plus classification accuracy.

Ablation study (Table 2) isolates each component (intra-region aggregation, hierarchical prototypes, fine-to-coarse fusion) and shows consistent gains on all three metrics, supporting the design choices.
The 'plug-in' experiments adding prototype learning to existing VPT methods (VPT-Deep, E2VPT, Gated Prompt Tuning) demonstrate generality of the core idea beyond the full IVPT framework.

Application to Gleason-2019 pathology images shows potential practical value in a safety-critical domain, and qualitative results on Stanford Cars and the hierarchical region maps (Figure 6) provide intuitive evidence for the fine-to-coarse semantics claim.
The paper is generally well written and organized, with clear motivation of the three challenges (region-prompt grounding, inter-concept relationships, category-agnostic sharing).
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on existing components: the part-shaping losses are directly borrowed from PDiscoNet [1], the evaluation metrics and protocol from Huang et al. [18], and prototype-based interpretability is a well-explored idea. The novelty is mainly in the combination with VPT and the hierarchical layer-wise structure, which is somewhat incremental.

Human-understandability of the learned concepts is asserted but never validated with a human study; interpretability is judged only by consistency/stability scores and qualitative visualizations, so the central claim of 'human-understandable semantic concepts' remains weakly supported.

Quantitative results are confined to a single dataset (CUB-200-2011); Gleason-2019 and Stanford Cars results are purely qualitative, limiting the breadth of empirical evidence for the interpretability claims.

IVPT trails Huang et al. [18] in consistency score on DinoV2-S (63.5 vs 65.7), and the explanation (limited model capacity) is speculative and untested; the advantage over the strongest baseline is not uniform.

No analysis of computational overhead: CRD, IFA, fusion layers, and part-shaping losses add significant cost relative to vanilla VPT, whose main selling point is parameter/compute efficiency. Training/inference cost and memory comparisons are missing.

Hyperparameter sensitivity (number of prototypes per layer 17/14/11/8, n=4, loss weights all set to 1) is not explored; there is no justification or sensitivity analysis for the hierarchical configuration.
The method relies on in-domain concept prototypes (acknowledged as a limitation), restricting applicability to diverse domains; no cross-domain or out-of-distribution experiments are provided.

Some design details are under-specified in the main text (e.g., how background grouping interacts with the classification head, how Eq. 8's argmax masking interacts with gradients), requiring reference to the supplementary material.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-explored question—interpretability of visual prompt tuning—rather than only of fully fine-tuned or conventionally trained networks.
The framework is clearly described, with well-defined modules (Concept Region Discovery, Intra-region Feature Aggregation, fine-to-coarse hierarchical fusion) and a coherent training objective.
Experiments are reasonably comprehensive across multiple backbone choices (DeiT-S/B, DinoV2-S/B/L), and the ablation study in Table 2 isolates the contribution of each component.

The use of established interpretability metrics (consistency and stability scores from Huang et al.) with keypoint-based ground truth provides a quantitative basis for comparing against part-prototype baselines, and IVPT shows gains over most of them.
Demonstrating that the prototype-learning scheme can be plugged into existing VPT methods (VPT, E2VPT, Gated Prompt Tuning) increases the practical utility of the idea.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core machinery is largely an adaptation of existing techniques to a new setting—the part-shaping losses are taken directly from PDiscoFormer [1], prototype similarity via negative squared Euclidean distance follows prior part-discovery works, and Gumbel-Softmax grouping is standard. The main contribution is the integration into VPT plus a hierarchical grouping scheme, which feels incremental.

Quantitative evaluation is confined to a single dataset (CUB-200-2011). Gleason-2019 and Stanford Cars results are qualitative only, so claims of broad applicability, including in the safety-critical medical domain emphasized in the introduction, are not supported quantitatively.

The interpretability gains are not uniformly superior: IVPT lags behind Huang et al. [18] in consistency for DinoV2-S, and the paper's explanation ('limited capacity of smaller models') is speculative and not validated by any experiment.

The interpretability metrics themselves are borrowed, and there is no human study or downstream task-based evaluation to substantiate the claim that the explanations are genuinely more useful or faithful to the model's decision process.

Important design and robustness questions are unaddressed or deferred: equal weighting (weight=1) of all loss terms with no sensitivity analysis in the main text, no analysis of computational/parameter overhead relative to vanilla VPT, and no ablation on the number of prototypes per layer or the number of fused prompts n.

The hierarchical structure motivation (fine semantics in shallow layers, coarse in deep layers) is asserted rather than empirically grounded; Figure 6 shows a few cherry-picked examples rather than a systematic validation of cross-layer semantic granularity.
Accuracy improvements over baselines (e.g., 90.8 vs. 90.7 for DinoV2-L) are marginal and likely within run-to-run variance; no error bars or multiple-seed results are reported.
The claimed advantage of category-agnostic prototypes over category-specific ones is central to the narrative but is never directly tested against a category-specific variant in the VPT setting.

strengths: Clear and relevant problem: interpretability of visual prompt tuning is underexplored, and the paper provides the first systematic attempt to bridge part-prototype interpretability with the VPT paradigm, which is a meaningful gap.

Well-motivated design: the hierarchical (fine-to-coarse) prototype structure across layers, category-agnostic prototypes, and the consistency loss linking fine-grained regions to coarse-grained ones are sensible and address the three stated limitations of prior part-prototype methods.

Reasonably comprehensive quantitative evaluation: five backbone configurations (DeiT-S/B, DinoV2-S/B/L), established interpretability metrics (consistency/stability from Huang et al.) using keypoint annotations that are inaccessible during training, plus classification accuracy.

Useful 'w/ Proto.' variants of existing VPT baselines isolate the contribution of the prototype learning scheme itself, providing evidence that the scheme is broadly applicable rather than only working in the full framework.
Ablation study (Table 2) cleanly decomposes the contributions of IFA, hierarchical prototypes, and fine-to-coarse fusion, showing each component helps.
Qualitative results span multiple domains (birds, cars, Gleason pathology), and the pathology visualizations plausibly align with clinically meaningful structures, supporting practical relevance.
The paper is well-organized and the method is described with sufficient formal detail (CRD, IFA, fusion, losses).
weaknesses: Limited novelty in isolation: the core components are largely assembled from prior work — part-shaping losses are taken directly from PDiscoFormer [1], the evaluation protocol from Huang et al. [18], part-prototype ideas from ProtoPNet/TesNet/ProtoTree, and Gumbel-Softmax grouping. The novelty is mainly the combination with VPT and the hierarchical structure, which is incremental.

Quantitative results are reported only on CUB-200-2011; Stanford Cars and Gleason-2019 are shown only as qualitative visualizations, so generalization of the quantitative interpretability gains across datasets/domains remains unverified. This weakens the claim of 'superior performance over existing interpretable methods'.

Potential technical soundness gaps: the argmax masking in Eq. (8) and the Gumbel-Softmax group assignment produce hard, non-differentiable (or only approximately differentiable) assignments; the paper does not explain how gradients flow through these operations (e.g., straight-through estimators) or discuss training stability.

All loss weights are fixed at 1 with no sensitivity analysis, and no discussion of how sensitive the results are to the number of prototypes per layer (17/14/11/8) and the choice of which four layers to annotate.

The 'first framework for interpretable visual prompt tuning' claim is overstated, given that the paper itself evaluates 'w/ Proto.' variants of VPT baselines and cites multi-modal interpretability approaches for prompts; the introduction does not compare against language-based prompt interpretability methods empirically.

No computational cost analysis: CRD and IFA applied at every annotated layer, at 518×518 resolution, add significant overhead relative to plain VPT; parameter/compute/latency comparisons against baselines are missing, which matters for a parameter-efficient-fine-tuning paper.

Concept semantics (e.g., 'glandular lumen', 'emblem/handle') are assigned post-hoc and only qualitatively; there is no human-subject or semantic evaluation confirming that the learned prototypes are genuinely human-understandable beyond the region-overlap metrics.

Fairness of comparisons is partially unclear: part-prototype baselines (ProtoPNet, TesNet, etc.) were designed for conventional training on much smaller images and may not be tuned for 518×518 DinoV2 features; the accuracy advantage of IVPT over prompt-tuning baselines may partly reflect backbone/protocol differences.
Key implementation details and additional analyses are deferred to supplementary material, limiting self-contained reproducibility of the main paper.
The limitation on in-domain concept prototypes is acknowledged but not explored; how IVPT behaves out-of-domain or with spurious-background concepts is untested.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored problem: interpretability of visual prompt tuning itself (rather than only final logits), which is a meaningful gap in the VPT literature.

The proposed framework is well-motivated: category-agnostic concept prototypes grounded in image regions, distributed across layers with fine-to-coarse fusion, plausibly combines attribution- and concept-based interpretability within a parameter-efficient tuning scheme.

Comprehensive evaluation: quantitative interpretability metrics (consistency/stability from Huang et al., 2023) plus accuracy on CUB across five backbones, generalization tests on PartImageNet and PASCAL-Part, qualitative studies on Gleason-2019, Stanford Cars, FGVCAircraft, and a human study.

Good ablations covering component contributions, number of prompted layers, and number of prototypes per layer, plus an honest computational overhead analysis (Appendix C) and candid failure-case analysis (Appendix G.3), which increases credibility.
The paper is clearly written and the method (CRD, IFA, cross-layer consistency loss, Gumbel-Softmax grouping) is described at sufficient detail for reproduction, with full loss definitions provided.
weaknesses: The core claim that prompts are linked to 'human-understandable semantic concepts' is only weakly supported: concepts have no language grounding or names at training time; the interpretation offered is region maps and importance scores, and concept naming appears only post-hoc in qualitative discussion. The human study (only 20 participants, thin methodology) partially addresses this but the headline framing overstates the evidence.

The reported near-perfect cross-layer IoU (>98-99%, Table 5) is suspicious and potentially self-fulfilling: the concept region consistency loss explicitly forces grouped fine-grained regions to match coarse-grained regions, so measuring their agreement is close to circular. Moreover, near-identical regions across layers contradicts the paper's central narrative of distinct fine-to-coarse semantic granularity, which should be discussed.

Novelty positioning as 'the first interpretable paradigm for VPT' is somewhat overclaimed given related work such as Prompt-CAM (Chowdhury et al., 2025) and part-prototype methods that could be adapted; the method itself is a fairly direct combination of PDiscoFormer-style part discovery (which is adopted wholesale for the part-shaping losses) with prompt tuning.

Accuracy gains over strong VPT baselines are modest (e.g., +0.1 to +0.6 on some backbones in Table 1), and IVPT lags Huang et al. on consistency for DinoV2-S; the significance of the improvements without error bars or multiple seeds is unclear.

Evaluation scope is narrow: interpretability metrics are evaluated only on CUB (with 10 concepts at the second-to-last layer, a design choice that conveniently matches the evaluation protocol) and the main quantitative table lacks confidence intervals; the dependence on learnable spatial bias maps tied to a fixed 37x37 resolution may hurt flexibility across input sizes, which is acknowledged but not analyzed.

Some presentation issues: the abstract's code link is incomplete, and the benefit of the cross-layer structure for downstream accuracy is small, making the practical cost-benefit (extra modules and losses) somewhat hard to assess.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: interpretability of visual prompts (rather than only final-layer features) in VPT, which is a reasonable and relevant research question.

Fairly comprehensive evaluation: five backbones (DeiT-S/B, DinoV2-S/B/L), multiple fine-grained datasets (CUB, PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part, plus qualitative results on Gleason-2019, Stanford Cars, FGVCAircraft), and ablations on components, number of layers, and prototype counts.
The comparison includes newly constructed 'w/ Proto.' variants of VPT baselines, which strengthens the attribution of gains to the proposed prototype mechanism rather than the backbone.

Includes both quantitative interpretability metrics (consistency/stability scores from Huang et al.), a human study, and failure-case analysis that honestly reports spurious prototype activations (e.g., 'bird legs' firing on branches).
The method is lightweight (only ~106K additional parameters), and training/inference overhead is quantified in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core machinery (negative squared-Euclidean prototype attention, spatial bias maps, and the entire part-shaping loss suite) is directly borrowed from PDiscoFormer (Aniraj et al., 2024), and the prototype-classification scheme follows ProtoPNet-style models. The genuinely new ingredients—cross-layer prototype allocation and the Gumbel-Softmax grouping/fusion—are heuristic design choices with thin motivation, and the paper overstates its contribution with 'first interpretable paradigm for VPT' claims despite related work such as Prompt-CAM.

The cross-layer alignment evaluation (Table 5, IoU >98%) is largely circular: the concept-region consistency loss (Eq. 8) explicitly optimizes for this alignment, so a near-perfect IoU between grouped fine-grained regions and coarse-grained regions only verifies that the loss was minimized, not that the hierarchy encodes semantically meaningful cross-layer structure. Similarly implausibly clean results appear in the human study (97.5% annotation accuracy, 4.7–4.8/5 on all dimensions with only 20 participants), which raises concerns about study design and reporting.

Interpretability comes at a real accuracy cost that is underplayed: on CUB with DinoV2-B, IVPT achieves 90.8 vs. 89.5–90.7 for prompt-tuning baselines but 88.1 for DinoV2-S; more importantly, the part-prototype baselines (ProtoPNet etc.) are weaker architectures trained under different regimes, making the head-to-head interpretability comparison unfair in IVPT's favor.

The claim that CUB is 'the only benchmark with part-level annotations required for fine-grained interpretability evaluation' is incorrect (PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part, and several others exist, and the paper itself later uses them), and the evaluation protocol on those datasets (a single representative point per part) is too weak to validate fine-grained grounding rigorously.

Reliance on consistency/stability scores as the primary interpretability evidence is questionable: these are indirect proxies (segmentation coherency and perturbation robustness) and do not establish that prototypes correspond to human-understandable concepts; the human study, which would provide the direct evidence, is small and relegated to the appendix.
The method unfreezes the class token, position embedding, register tokens, and distillation token, which weakens the parameter-efficiency framing central to the VPT setting.

Interpretability is validated almost exclusively on fine-grained classification; the generalization experiments (CIFAR-100, ImageNet, VLCS) are purely qualitative and provide no quantitative support for the breadth of the claims.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: interpretability of visual prompts themselves (rather than final features/logits) in prompt tuning, which is a timely topic

The framework is clearly motivated and well-structured, with a coherent pipeline (Concept Region Discovery + Intra-region Feature Aggregation + cross-layer prompt fusion) described with sufficient mathematical detail

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: five backbone variants, multiple datasets (CUB-200-2011, PartImageNet, PASCAL-Part), component-wise ablations (Table 3), hyperparameter ablations on layers/prototype counts (Table 4), qualitative visualizations across domains, failure-case analysis, and a human study

Fair comparison design: baselines include both part-prototype networks and VPT methods augmented with the authors' prototype mechanism ('w/ Proto.' rows), isolating the contribution of the full cross-layer design
Lightweight design: ~0.12% additional parameters and modest computational overhead, with an honest cost analysis in the appendix
Code availability and reasonable training details support reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited novelty in core components: the concept/region discovery mechanism and the entire part-shaping loss suite (orthogonality, equivariance, presence, entropy, TV losses) are directly adopted from PDiscoFormer (Aniraj et al., 2024), and the evaluation metrics come from Huang et al. (2023); the main novel elements are the cross-layer grouping (Gumbel-Softmax + KL consistency loss) and prompt fusion, which are relatively incremental

Circular validation of the cross-layer mechanism: Table 5 reports ~99% IoU between aggregated fine-grained regions and coarse-grained regions, but this alignment is directly optimized via the concept region consistency loss (Eq. 8); reporting near-perfect agreement on the very quantity the loss enforces is not independent evidence the hierarchy captures meaningful semantics, and such uniformly >98% values strongly suggest a trivial/degenerate solution rather than a discovery

The human study raises credibility concerns: 97.5% annotation accuracy and near-ceiling Likert scores (4.7–4.8/5) from only 20 participants, with no inter-annotator agreement, blinding protocol, task design, or statistical analysis reported; such uniformly positive results are unusual and under-supported

Unexplained inconsistencies in results: the paper concedes IVPT lags Huang et al. by 2.2% consistency on DinoV2-S, and the accuracy ordering across methods is not always consistent with the interpretability narrative; the 'first framework' claim is weakened by prior work like Prompt-CAM that also targets interpretable prompts

Evaluation scope is narrow for an interpretability claim: quantitative interpretability is evaluated mainly with two proxy metrics (consistency/stability) on part-annotated datasets; there is no quantitative faithfulness/completeness evaluation showing the explanations actually reflect the model's decision process, and the pathology results (Gleason-2019) are visualization-only

Hyperparameter sensitivity is underexplored in the main text: fixed settings (prototype counts 17/14/11/8, all loss weights = 1) appear hand-tuned, and the appendix ablation shows sharp performance drops outside this configuration (e.g., 5-layer cases), suggesting fragility

Some technical details are loosely specified, e.g., the appendix parameter analysis assumes 768-d prototypes for all backbones while DeiT-S uses 384-d, and Eq. 5 conflates softmax-normalized attention with an additive bias outside the normalized term, which is not a proper probability without further justification
